11	AJCR run 0072 s0008. The mkdir lock at `/tmp/claude-1001/ajcr-locks/lake.lock` has a careful
12	*acquire* recipe (reap only on proof of death) and a careless *release* (`rm -rf "$LOCK"`). I fell
13	through that hole: I removed the lock while its pidfile named pid 1212361, another lane's live
14	build — **having printed `ALIVE` for that pid one line earlier in my own output.**
15	
16	The mechanism is the part worth remembering. I had legitimately acquired the lock, and then **my
17	own shell was killed by a harness timeout while I held it.** On the next turn I reasoned "the lock
18	is mine and my holder is dead, so release it". In that interval a different lane had acquired it,
19	so the pid in the file had never been mine. No damage this time — but the lane whose build I
20	exposed correctly said that was timing luck, not a property of the reap.
21	
22	**Why:** every turn boundary is a window in which another lane can take the lock. A release
23	decided from remembered history is a write decided without a read.
24	
25	**How to apply:**
26	- Before `rm -rf "$LOCK"`, verify the pidfile still names your own pid:
27	  `[ "$(cat "$LOCK/pid" 2>/dev/null)" = "$$" ] && rm -rf "$LOCK"`.
28	- Never "repair" a mistaken removal by re-creating the directory with the other lane's pid — that
29	  makes the lock unreapable by its real owner and hides the incident. Report it and let the owner
30	  re-take it.
31	- **Prefer a hold that cannot outlive its own process**: run the build detached from a script that
32	  acquires, builds, and releases in the *same* process, so no turn boundary sits inside the hold.
33	- When your own output contradicts your plan, the output wins. I printed the refutation and acted
34	  on the plan anyway.

**CONFIRMED 2026-07-29 (run 0072 r5), and the detached-hold advice is now MANDATORY, not
preferred.** I held the lock in a foreground `Bash` call with an explicit `timeout 3000` and
`timeout: 3400000`. The harness capped it at **10 minutes** regardless and killed the shell
mid-hold — so the "acquire, build, release in one foreground call" shape *cannot* work here for
any build longer than 10 min, which is every root build. My dead pid was then correctly reaped
by a waiting lane. No damage, but only because the reap recipe is careful.

So: never hold this lock from a foreground tool call. Write the acquire/build/release script to
a file and launch it with `nohup setsid … &`, then watch it with a Monitor or an until-loop on
its status log. The hold then lives in a process the harness does not own, and no turn boundary
or timeout sits inside it.
